lines: The identical update statement, run three separate times, with one setting changed in between each run.
What changes is REPLICA IDENTITY, the thing that decides how much of the old row gets logged alongside the new one.
Under one setting the before-image fills in completely. Under another it shrinks to a single column. Under the third, it's empty.
Before I show you what the slot actually does, answer this.
I read the same slot twice, with a function that only peeks, never confirms anything was received.
Does the second peek come back empty, since the slot already showed me that change once, or does it come back identical to the first?
answer: Saying it comes back empty assumes the slot is keeping score of what it's shown you, just from the act of reading.
But a slot's position only moves when a read explicitly confirms it. Peeking confirms nothing, so nothing has changed from the slot's point of view.

lines: Here's what decoding is actually doing underneath both of those readings.
The write-ahead log already records every change a transaction makes, in the order each transaction finishes, not the order each one starts.
Decoding just turns those storage-level records back into a readable insert, update, or delete, in that same finishing order.
I ran that three-setting comparison against this sandbox's own real database, not a mock of REPLICA IDENTITY's behavior.
Under the setting that logs only the primary key, the before-image shows just that one column, nothing else about the row.
Under the setting that logs everything, the identical update's before-image carries every column the row had, whether or not that column actually changed.
Now here's why a slot can ever show you the same change twice in the first place.
A slot's own position is written to disk only when the server checkpoints, not after every single change it hands out.
Between two checkpoints, whatever the slot thinks it has already delivered only exists in memory, not anywhere durable yet.
I ran that exact unconfirmed peek twice against the real slot, back to back.
Both reads came back with the identical decoded change, down to the byte, because neither one ever told the slot the change was received.
That's not a bug in the slot. That's the whole reason a consumer has to be able to handle seeing the same change again.
A slot actually tracks two separate positions, and they protect two separate things.
The restart position is the oldest point in the log the server still can't throw away, because this slot might still need it.
The confirmed flush position is simply how far the consumer has actually acknowledged reading to. One is a promise kept; the other is a promise made.
I measured both of those positions directly, before and after a real confirmed read on this sandbox's own slot.
After the read, the confirmed flush position had moved forward, exactly as far as the consumer had actually acknowledged.
The restart position hadn't moved at all. The gap between the two of them is log the server is still keeping, on this slot's behalf, for no reason yet.
Step back, and everything shown so far is really one server's own private bookkeeping.
What REPLICA IDENTITY logs, whether a read repeats, and where the two positions sit are all facts about this one PostgreSQL server, and only this one.
None of that bookkeeping travels anywhere on its own. It stays exactly where it was created.
Here's what a single server's own bookkeeping doesn't cover.
Everything shown so far lives on one PostgreSQL server. What does a consumer actually need so it keeps working if that one server fails over to another?
answer: Saying a slot already survives its own crash is true, but a crash isn't the same thing as a failover to a different machine entirely.
A slot lives only on the server that made it, so a standby needs to be told to track it, or the primary needs to keep a synchronized copy there in advance.
